In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence for an association between dental practitioners' density and access to dental health care for the elderly is inconclusive.
the dental care system in the Netherlands has a relatively high density of dentists, but the access to dental care is low for elderly people with a low socioeconomic position.

the use of the term'social determinants of health' in the field of dental health is not only justified by the evidence but also that the term is a useful concept to understand and explain the social patterning of oral health and dental care.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dental care system is not well adapted to the elderly, and that the elderly are not well served by the current system.
the elderly are less likely to have dental care than younger age groups and that this inequality is larger for the elderly with lower socio-economic position (SEP).
the dental workforce is not distributed equally across regions and that this is associated with access to dental care and with socio-economic inequality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dental care needs of the elderly population are not met by the existing dental workforce, especially in the rural areas.
there are many different ways to define the concept of "dental care," and that these different definitions can have significant effects on how we understand access to dental care.
the dental care utilization gap between the elderly with and without functional limitations is smaller in regions with higher dental practitioner densities.
